Most of the advantage depends on the inference-time loop, and cross-brief distinctiveness falls slightly below that of the base model, the only success criterion not met.

papers.title: AI Tool Adoption and Loyalty among Product, Industrial, and UX/UI Designers across the Double Diamond
papers.abstract: Designers share many AI tools, yet their roles produce different work. This survey compared 337 Product, Industrial and UX/UI Designers from 40 countries and regions across the four phases of the Double Diamond. It measured AI adoption, breadth and frequency, tool function and the number of tools named per phase. A tool was loyal when a role picked it in all four phases. Industrial Designers adopted AI less often (73.9% against 88.2% and 87.9%), a gap that went with physical projects once project type and country were held constant. Of 60 AI tools, 25 were common to all three roles and carried at least 90% of each role's picks. Tool function differed by role, most of all in Develop. A few loyal tools carried about half of the picks, led by ChatGPT. Tool counts fell across the phases in every role. A hurdle model found a Phase x Role interaction for using AI in a phase (p = 0.041), which was not shown for the number of tools (p = 0.080). Predicted adoption among UX/UI Designers fell from 87.2% in Define to 43.9% in Develop. Support for designers needs one shared core, role-specific tools and most attention in Develop.

papers.title: EVIDENT: Evaluating Evidence Grounding in GUI Agents
papers.abstract: GUI agents are increasingly evaluated by whether they complete web tasks, but surface success can hide a critical failure: the final answer may not be supported by evidence observed during navigation. We introduce EVIDENT, an evidence-driven benchmark for evaluating whether GUI agents ground their decisions in observable web evidence. EVIDENT contains 220 real-world English and Korean tasks spanning semantic grounding, contextual inference, and visual grounding, each paired with human-curated evidence metadata specifying what must be verified. We further separate surface task completion from evidence-grounded success using three metrics: TSR, ESR, and GSR, which respectively measure outcome success, required evidence observation, and claim-level evidence support. Experiments on commercial and open-source GUI agents reveal substantial gaps between surface success and evidence-grounded success, especially in contextual and visual tasks. These results show that current evaluations can overestimate agent reliability and highlight the need to assess not only whether agents answer, but whether they verify.

papers.title: PromptPoseFX: Authoring Pose-Driven Visual Effects through Augmented Prompting and Interactive Refinement
papers.abstract: Human pose-driven visual effects offer a compelling way for enhancing video expressiveness and storytelling. Authoring such effects with traditional video editing tools is a complex and time-consuming task that requires considerable technical expertise and manual effort. While generative AI models can simplify the workflow by reducing manual scripting through language-driven generation, existing approaches suffer from imprecise alignment between visual effects and pose data, failure to preserve original video content, and limited support for fine-grained, iterative refinement. To address these challenges, we present PromptPoseFX, an interactive system that allows creators to author pose-driven visual effects through augmented language prompts and interactive refinement. Our system leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to translate high-level user intent into parameterized procedural graphics scripts, automatically mapping pose-tracking data to specific effect parameters, allowing precise alignment with human motion. This script-based approach manages effects as independent layers, thereby preserving the original content of the underlying video. To reduce language ambiguity, our interface offers controls across spatial, temporal, and parameter domains, enabling the precise, intuitive, and iterative authoring of pose-driven visual effects. We evaluated PromptPoseFX through a comparative study against a text-only LLM interface, followed by an exploratory study. In the comparative study, participants rated PromptPoseFX significantly higher than the text-only baseline on measures of perceived control and precision. The exploratory study examined usability and creativity support in open-ended authoring tasks.

papers.title: Straight to the Product: What Online Retailers Miss When Shoppers Ask AI First
papers.abstract: When people ask an AI assistant what to buy, what happens next at the store? We link the same people's assistant conversations to their later browsing at twenty large online retailers. People go to the product the assistant named: among shoppers who had not visited the store in the past week, visits to the named product within a day rise from 0.02 to 2.07 per 100 answers (+2.0 points [1.7, 2.4]), and on days with a product-page visit at the store, 44% show a product from their own answer, against 1.5% for a matched answer given to someone else. The result replicates in a separate five-month period. Few arrive through the assistant's link: 89% of visits carry no sign of it, and 54% follow a web search, the same share as their usual visits. When a search comes just before the first visit, it names the answer's product 28% of the time (1% in earlier weeks), as if the search box were an address bar. The chat names the product; the store logs a search. Once there, shoppers keep browsing. We propose product follow-through, the share of answers followed by a visit to the product they named, as a way to evaluate shopping assistants and agents by what people do next: it needs no referral data or provider logs and can be computed for each assistant.

papers.title: Supporting Community Members Navigating Reentry with Revisable Future Envisioning
papers.abstract: Future-planning tools often treat agency as individual and leave out the institutional conditions that shape how aspirations become action. We examine this tension in the context of reentry from incarceration and recovery from substance use disorder, through a partnership with a nonprofit organization. Building on participants' physical vision-board practices, we designed a digital future-envisioning tool that helps users represent current circumstances, desired futures, and pathways that connect goals to concrete resources. We draw on data from three workshops involving 18 participants and follow-up interviews with 10 participants to examine how they used future envisioning within a fragmented support system. Participants described reentry and recovery as ongoing processes in which the everyday work of staying stable was central to progress. Envisioning futures supported this work by surfacing constraints and interdependencies, by reframing personal strengths and institutional supports as assets, and by helping participants move from abstract hopes toward articulated goals and contingent plans. We theorize revision as maintenance work and conclude with design implications for community-embedded interactive systems that support revisable, dependency-aware planning.

papers.title: "Can a Robot Really Care About Me?" How Perceiving a Tutor as Human or AI Affects Computer Science Students' Attitudes and Experiences
papers.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence can reproduce many instructional and social behaviors of human tutors, but students may interpret those behaviors differently depending on who they believe is providing them. We examined how perceived tutor identity shapes students' evaluations of instructional feedback, satisfaction of psychological needs according to Self-Determination Theory, and their communication strategies with tutors. In a within-subjects Wizard-of-Oz study, 27 introductory computer science students completed two text-based tutoring sessions involving Python code-explanation problems. Participants were told one tutor was human and the other was AI, although the same human provided feedback in both conditions. We found participants evaluated both tutors favorably and reported few consistent differences in the instructional value of the feedback. However, participants frequently questioned whether AI could genuinely care about them, which corresponded with the human tutor having higher scores of relatedness need satisfaction. Human presence offered connection and accountability for some participants but introduced anxiety in others. Participants also reported communicating more casually with the human tutor and more explicitly with the AI tutor. These findings suggest complementary roles for human and AI tutoring and highlight the importance of considering psychological needs alongside instructional quality.

papers.title: Sidewalk Stewards: A Visual Analytics Approach for Interactive Topology Repair of Sidewalk Networks
papers.abstract: Accurate pedestrian network data is foundational to urban accessibility, routing, and infrastructure planning, yet such data remains scarce and difficult to produce at scale. Automated extraction pipelines have made significant strides by leveraging computer vision to derive sidewalk networks from aerial imagery, and have seen real-world adoption by municipalities seeking cost-effective inventory solutions. Yet, these pipelines consistently produce topological errors (e.g., disconnected components, dangling edges, missed connections, malformed intersections) that undermine the utility of the extracted networks for routing and accessibility analysis. Correcting these errors requires situated human judgment that global automated repair strategies cannot replicate, yet practitioners currently lack dedicated tools to support this work efficiently. We present Sidewalk Stewards, a visual analytics system that bridges the gap between automated extraction and a deployment-ready pedestrian network. Sidewalk Stewards detects candidate topology errors, supports interactive user-guided correction through coordinated spatial views, and provides real-time quality feedback as edits are applied. We evaluate Sidewalk Stewards through a comparative user study, case studies across cities, and a quantitative evaluation. Compared with conventional workflows, the system facilitates error identification and enables faster and more complete correction. The case studies illustrate the workflow across different urban contexts, and the quantitative evaluation shows that a small number of user corrections can enhance multiple sidewalk quality metrics. Sidewalk Stewards is available at urbantk.org/sidewalk.

papers.title: Vibe Interventions: Can Users Personalize and Iterate Their Way to Behavior Change?
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models allow a working application to be generated from natural-language description, and is referred to as generative user interfaces. Their application to behavior change is unexplored, and we provide one of the first controlled investigations of it. We distinguish two components of authorship: iteration, the revision of a generated artifact in natural language, and personalization, the conditioning of generation on stated context. In a pre-registered between-subjects experiment (N = 300, 60 per condition), we crossed these two factors and added a static intervention as a control, yielding five conditions; participants stated a goal and received a generated intervention. The personalized generative condition ranked highest on every self-report outcome, including ownership, satisfaction, and intended adoption. Randomized iteration had no detectable effect, and higher revision counts were negatively associated with evaluative ratings. This work establishes which component of authorship carries motivational value in generative behavior change tools.

papers.title: Reveal: A Provenance-Aware System for Multimodal Urban Data Exploration
papers.abstract: Urban sensing initiatives increasingly produce multimodal datasets that combine visual and textual information to capture city characteristics and subjective factors such as safety, comfort, and accessibility. Yet, analyzing such data at scale remains difficult, as manual inspection is unfeasible and automated methods struggle to interpret subjective cues and uncover relationships across diverse data modalities. Moreover, existing workflows rarely make exploration steps explicit, hindering reproducibility. To address these challenges, we introduce Reveal, a provenance-aware visual analytics system for exploring heterogeneous urban data. Reveal enables users to build dataflows by combining text and image searches across coordinated views, chaining queries into pipelines, and applying set operations within an exploration diagram while capturing analytical provenance. We evaluate Reveal through two case studies focused on accessibility and walkability.

papers.title: From XR Sketches to CAD: Preserving Design Intent with AI
papers.abstract: Extended reality (XR) allows designers to sketch shapes directly in 3D, but converting these sketches into editable, feature-based CAD requires interpreting their intent. A sketch may contain drawing errors, intended features, and design choices that remain open. Correcting every irregularity risks erasing intended features, while automatic completion may impose choices the designer has not made. We argue that AI should add precision without overriding design intent, considering both the resulting shape and how the CAD model behaves during later edits. To guide this process, we propose a conceptual framework that distinguishes errors from intentions in individual sketch properties and relates them to correction, preservation, and exploration in editable CAD. We also outline five research directions for sketch interpretation, CAD construction, and evaluation, with testable hypotheses for selected questions.

papers.title: DoF-Query Transformer for Adaptive Fusion of Egocentric Vision and Forearm HD-sEMG in Continuous Hand Kinematics
papers.abstract: Continuous and accurate estimation of human hand kinematics is important not only for intuitive human-machine interaction, but also for capturing fine-grained human manipulation demonstrations that can provide action supervision for embodied-intelligence datasets and dexterous robot learning. However, individual sensing modalities may be insufficient for reliable estimation under varying operating conditions. We present a finger-unencumbered multimodal framework for continuous regression of 20 hand joint angles from egocentric RGB images and 128-channel forearm high-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG). The framework combines a Vision Transformer-based visual encoder, a Transformer-based EMG encoder, and a degree of freedom (DoF) query Transformer fusion decoder. To account for the varying informativeness of visual and EMG cues across joint DoFs and input conditions, the decoder assigns a separate learnable query to each DoF, enabling DoF-specific and context-adaptive fusion of the two modalities. The framework was evaluated on synchronized multimodal data from 10 participants. Averaged across participants, the proposed fusion model achieved a mean coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of $0.88$ and a mean absolute error (MAE) of $2.80^\circ$, compared with $0.82$ and $3.21^\circ$ for the vision-only model and $0.68$ and $5.13^\circ$ for the EMG-only model. It also outperformed the evaluated representative unimodal baselines and alternative fusion designs. DoF-wise analyses showed larger fusion gains for visually ambiguous joints and viewing conditions, while synthetic visual occlusion demonstrated greater robustness than vision-only estimation. These results highlight the complementary value of egocentric vision and forearm HD-sEMG for capturing fine-grained human hand kinematics, with potential applications in human demonstration acquisition and dexterous robot learning.

papers.title: A Line is Not Just a Line: Visualizing Harmonious Complex Line Sets
papers.abstract: Line is a foundational building block in visual design for traditional media and computer graphics. Controlled variation in line quality can be used to define form, create abstractions, distinguish categories, control affect, and more. Yet, when it comes to computer graphics visualizations of science, particularly those built upon 3D computer graphics, too often a line is just a line. This portfolio presents a series of visual design studies and lessons learned that explore the diverse character of line that might be useful for 3D visualizations. The imagery begins to show how more sophisticated use of this powerful visual building block could increase the clarity of data visualizations while also bringing a human, handcrafted aesthetic that reinforces the people and impacts behind scientific climate data.

papers.title: Cyber-Secure Wearable, Ultra-Low-Power Networked Sensors for Soldier Health Monitoring: Insights from the CAPSARII project
papers.abstract: The CAPSARII project advances a cyber-secure, ultra-low-power wearable platform and Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) framework to support real-time monitoring of military personnel and data-driven decision support. The architecture integrates smart-textile sensing, a body/squad area mesh, edge-deployed AI on secure RISC-V microcontrollers, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning and comparative studies. Two representative use cases--pilot fatigue and warfighters operating in harsh environments--guide requirements, validation, and interface design (including HUD and haptic feedback). As an initial step toward embedded models, we benchmark stress classification on a public wearable dataset: tree-ensemble baselines achieve state-of-the-art performance for accuracy and F1 (e.g., XGBoost: $Accuracy=0.901\!\pm\!0.023$, $F1=0.920\!\pm\!0.019$), while a feature-based Transformer attains the highest AUC ($0.963\!\pm\!0.025$), informing feature-engineering and compression choices for edge deployment. Building on these results, CAPSARII employs HW/SW co-design, model compression (pruning, quantization, distillation), and precision tuning to meet stringent energy and memory budgets; it further investigates Processing-in-Memory accelerators for future efficiency gains. A structured gap analysis highlights the remaining challenges: establishing validation standards for physiological signal quality and textile durability; achieving low-latency, scalable BAN/SAN communications under mobility and interference; and deploying hybrid lightweight/post-quantum cryptography with robust device identity and side-channel resilience on constrained endpoints. By consolidating these elements into a coherent, secure IoBT stack, CAPSARII delineates a practical roadmap from laboratory baselines to mission-ready soldier monitoring in both training and operational scenarios.

papers.title: WL-Headset Law: Projecting Future Headset Evolution from a Decade of Display and Mass Data
papers.abstract: Tracking a decade of headset display and mass changes can inform forecasts. However, comparing headset resolution requires pixels per degree (PPD), which is often unreported and estimated using unclear assumptions. Therefore, we compile the open-source, evidence-linked HMD Resolution and Mass Database (HRMD) with 241 configurations from 2016--2026 and introduce structure- and axis-aware robust calibration (SARC) to estimate missing central PPD. Compared with official PPD, SARC reduces PPD estimation error from 14.8% for traditional geometric estimation to 3.2%. Based on HRMD, we introduce the Weight-Linked Headset Law (WL-Headset Law), which models PPD by year, mass, and category. The law reveals 7.4% annual PPD growth at fixed mass and category. Meanwhile, head-worn mass fell by 6.5% annually after category adjustment. At an eyeglass-like mass of 30g, the law projects average central PPD of 60 (normal visual acuity) around 2035 and 120 (higher acuity) around 2044 if trends persist.

papers.title: Turning Errors into Successes: Designing LLM Tutoring Around Scaffolded Error Correction
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) could make personalized tutoring available at scale, but it remains unclear how they can best support the instructional processes that make one-on-one instruction effective. We compared two ways of using LLMs after students make errors: providing personalized explanations of those errors, or engaging students in additional cycles of scaffolded practice and feedback, with a Socratic tutor guiding students toward the correct answer. In a preregistered online experiment, 400 adults practiced setting up constraint equations and, after each attempt, received the correct answer, a generic explanation, a personalized LLM explanation of their error, or Socratic tutoring. Socratic tutoring helped: participants resolved 64% of their errors through the dialogue and scored 0.24 SD higher on practice-aligned posttest questions than those who received generic or personalized explanations. Socratic participants also found the session more interesting, less frustrating, and less costly, even though it took nearly twice as long. In contrast, we found no evidence of a benefit of personalized explanations over generic ones, and neither type of explanation reliably outperformed simply seeing the correct answer. These findings suggest that LLM tutors may add the most value not by explaining errors more precisely but by helping students correct those errors themselves through scaffolded practice. This pattern fits a mastery-experience account of tutoring, in which an effective tutor notices when a student is struggling, steps in with guidance, and works with the student until the struggle resolves into success. AI tutors may be most effective when designed around this principle.

papers.title: VoiceGuard: An Audio-Native LLM-VLA Pipeline for Wheelchair-Mounted Assistive Manipulation
papers.abstract: Wheelchair-mounted robotic arms can help people with limited upper-limb mobility reach and manipulate everyday objects, but operating them typically requires stepwise joystick control and frequent mode switching. Natural-language interfaces could let users express task-level goals, yet they must handle ambiguous requests, distinguish commands from nearby conversation, and support interruption. We present VoiceGuard, a voice interface that separates spoken intent from robot execution through structured request validation and a local stop mechanism. On-device detectors handle the wake phrase and stop commands, an audio-native large language model (LLM) routes each request into a structured function packet, a rule-based ToolDispatcher accepts, rejects, or clarifies the packet, and a SmolVLA vision-language-action (VLA) policy executes accepted tasks on a low-cost SO-101 arm. Preliminary tests showed that the system correctly handled 55 of 60 voice commands, including ambiguous and non-directed utterances, completed 16 of 20 deliveries, and stopped the arm on all 20 stop commands with a median latency of 210 ms. We demonstrate the feasibility of combining flexible spoken input with constrained task execution and local interruption for wheelchair-mounted assistive manipulation.

papers.title: From Companion to Guardian: Designing an Emergency Support System Using a Quadruped Robot for Older Adults
papers.abstract: As older adults increasingly live alone, emergency support becomes an important function for home companion robots. In Australia, demand for the care and support workforce is projected to nearly double between 2020-21 and 2049-50. Service robots such as robot dogs may support older adults by combining everyday companionship with assistance when human support is not immediately available. We present the design and implementation of a domestic companion-robot system on a Unitree Go1 quadruped platform that combines companionship with emergency awareness and response. The system uses a three-stage interaction model consisting of companion, danger-awareness, and emergency modes. A rule-based escalation policy combines signs detected from visual and speech input to determine the current risk level and adjust how long the robot waits for the user to confirm safety before entering emergency mode. Additional detected signs can shorten this waiting time. Users can confirm safety, request immediate help, stop robot motion, or reset the system. We verified the implemented decision rules and escalation timing through 105 automated trials and 25 staged physical trials. Additional visual evidence shortened the waiting time, and the system entered emergency mode when the waiting time ended without confirmation.

papers.title: Sangyadhi: An Analytical Framework for Diagnosing and Investigating Collective Care
papers.abstract: While HCI has expanded from Personal to Family Informatics, researchers still lack a critical analytical vocabulary to diagnose what truly constitutes a collective care context. We introduce Sangyadhi, an analytical sociotechnical framework that synthesizes Situated Action, Distributed Cognition, the Capabilities Approach, and Actor-Network Theory to investigate multi-actor care ecologies. The framework articulates four interdependent analytical lenses: contextual grounding, distributed responsibility, trust-mediated sharing, and collaborative actionability. To demonstrate its diagnostic utility, we apply Sangyadhi to critically audit a decade of HCI digital health literature across self-tracking, family informatics, and clinical AI---surfacing structural omissions in how shifting authority, dynamic trust, and AI escalation are conceptualized. Ultimately, the goal of Sangyadhi is to equip researchers with an analytical blueprint for diagnosing observed care contexts, structuring field inquiries, and evaluating future technologies.

papers.title: Developing JEEVHITAA: Designing and Evaluating a Human-Centered AI Ecosystem for Collective Care
papers.abstract: Health management is often a collective activity, involving family members and close relations in monitoring, interpreting, and coordinating care. Yet, most digital health technologies remain individual-centric, offering limited support for the distributed responsibilities and negotiated information sharing that characterize collective care. We present JEEVHITAA, a human-centered AI ecosystem designed to address this gap. Drawing on existing literature on collective health practices, we identify key requirements and translate them into a canonical ontology and a versioned data schema that underpin a mobile ecosystem integrating wearable data, role-aware sharing, granular access controls, auditable histories, and AI-assisted health summarization and verification. We first evaluated core system primitives using 1,000 ontology-driven synthetic care circles to test data visibility and information-processing workflows. We then conducted a controlled lab study with 13 subject--care-actor dyads (26 participants), combining task-based interactions, semi-structured interviews, the System Usability Scale, and component-level usability assessments. Findings indicate positive perceptions of usability and highlight the value of granular sharing and transparent information provenance. They also expose tensions between reciprocal transparency and surveillance, and between AI-mediated assistance and potentially intrusive notifications. We discuss implications for designing accountable, context-sensitive technologies that support collective care.

papers.title: LLM Facilitation of Group Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Human groups often fail to integrate information distributed across their members, converging on incorrect decisions. We ask whether large language models (LLMs) can help groups reach the correct decision in such settings. In an online, chat-based experiment, 138 three-person groups (N = 414) completed a hidden-profile hiring task that required selecting the best candidate using public information available to all group members and private information available only to individual members. The randomized human-subject experiment included three conditions: no facilitation, an individual-level LLM that messaged each member privately, and a group-level LLM that messaged the whole group. The LLM facilitation consisted of adaptive interventions that summarized the discussion, nudged quiet members, and played devil's advocate. The LLM did not know which candidate was correct. Both LLM conditions significantly increased the rate at which groups reached consensus on the correct candidate, from 32.6% without facilitation to 56.5% with LLM facilitation. LLM-facilitated groups exchanged more consensus messages signaling agreement on the group's choice. Participants in the group-level condition also disclosed significantly more information about the correct candidate, whereas those receiving individual-level facilitation repeated public information less often. Finally, group-level facilitation received more favorable usability ratings than individual-level facilitation. These results show that LLMs can deliver adaptive, theory-informed interventions that improve group decision-making, and that the design of these interventions may shape how people respond to them.

papers.title: Are Average Estimates in Line Graphs Biased Toward Areas of Higher Variability?
papers.abstract: When estimating the average value of a data series in line graphs, do viewers systematically overweight regions of higher variability? This is the question that Moritz et al. [14] set out to answer, and across two preregistered experiments they reported evidence for a bias they termed variability overweighting. Using their released data and code, I first reproduce their reported analysis, then ask whether their inference survives an equally valid analytic choice: measuring estimation error against the average of the displayed marks of each stimulus, rather than against a reference series that, for one mark type, is never shown. Under this alternative operationalization, the effect is substantially reduced and, for one mark type, reverses. Splitting the analysis by whether variability appears in the upper or lower region of the graph further reveals an asymmetry that the original direction-corrected analysis collapses away. I argue that the deeper issue is what verbal theories leave unspecified. When a theory is silent about which operationalization it requires, the metric ends up doing the theory's arguing for it. I close with a discussion of what reproduction and reanalysis are for: not verdicts on truth, but instruments for making analytic contingency visible and for forcing theories to say more.

papers.title: Behavioral Assurance for Socially Deployed AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.

papers.title: Towards Informed Autonomy Design: Understanding the Interplay of Function Characteristics and Autonomy Preferences in Automotive Agents
papers.abstract: Proactive, autonomous interactions receive high interest in the field of intelligent assistants, including the automotive domain. A central challenge, however, is identifying appropriate levels of autonomy for different functions while maintaining user acceptance and trust. This work examines how function characteristics relate to suitable autonomy levels and whether these relationships generalize across functions. We conducted an expert workshop to define autonomy levels and identify relevant function characteristics. We then collected data from 126 participants, who rated 14 in-vehicle functions regarding autonomy preferences and function characteristics, from which we trained machine learning models to predict appropriate autonomy levels. Building on our findings, we developed our prototypical Autonomy Design Assistant that supports designers in making autonomy-related decisions, which we evaluated qualitatively with nine experts. Our results suggest that function characteristics can rank functions by their suitable level of autonomy and thereby guide more informed autonomy design decisions, whereas predictions for individual users remain uncertain.

papers.title: Security Authentication as Protective Friction: Understanding the Dual Effects of Authentication Measures in e-Government Platform
papers.abstract: E-Government platforms, such as government credit platforms, handle highly sensitive personal data, requiring stringent security authentication (e.g., facial recognition, multi-factor verification) that protects users but impedes their experience. Drawing on Tomalin's (2023) e-friction typology and the emerging literature on beneficial design friction, we reconceptualize these authentication measures as protective friction, a theoretically distinct form of non-elective, overt, impeding e-friction that serves a security-enhancing function. We propose a dual-pathway model in which protective friction simultaneously reduces privacy-security risk perception (protection pathway) and increases effort cost (cost pathway), with self-efficacy moderating only the risk pathway. This differential pattern suggests that what matters is not users' ability to overcome friction, but their comprehension of its protective purpose, a construct we term protective mechanism comprehension. We outline a mixed-methods research design combining a survey of platform users and semi-structured interviews with platform staff at a Chinese municipal credit center to test this model. This research-in-progress contributes to IS theory by extending e-friction research from conceptual typology to empirical investigation, identifying when security friction becomes beneficial rather than burdensome.

papers.title: Decomposing the Associative Chain: Schema-Based Mediation Supports Expression and Understanding in Human-AI Music Co-creation
papers.abstract: Users cannot reliably translate their creative intents into AI-generated music. We contend that the root of this difficulty lies in associative divergence: associations between narratives and musical features are overly remote, and users lack a visible mediation structure to negotiate them. To address this, we introduce five core schema groups as cognitive mediation and propose a bidirectional schema-based framework. Its forward pathway decomposes narrative-to-music associations into staged mappings, while its reverse pathway provides structured interpretations from music back to narrative. Findings from two user studies(N = 188; N = 60) show that the framework led to clearer creative expression and greater perceived control, improved the comprehensibility of generated music, especially for unconventional pieces. Furthermore, it supported cultural and affective thinking while helping users locate associative divergence. Our work points toward better creative intent alignment in human-AI music co-creation.

papers.title: ANCHOR: A Port-Hamiltonian Model for Forecasting Team Dynamics in Human-in-the-Loop Systems
papers.abstract: Cyber-physical-human systems close a loop around people by sensing human behavior, predict it and act on it. Human teams are a natural target, because collaboration breaks down in ways that a timely prompt could prevent. Collaborative mixed reality makes this loop practical, since each headset senses who speaks, where its wearer looks and who stands together, and it can deliver a light prompt. In this loop, the headsets are sensors, the prompts are actuators and the team is the plant. Closing the loop needs a plant model that is small enough to learn from few teams, safe to iterate and readable by a designer. We propose ANCHOR, which models a team as a ball in an energy bowl. The bottom of the bowl is where the team rests, and it is set by the team's recent behavior, its own history and other teams. Formally, ANCHOR is a switched port-Hamiltonian system with 52 parameters, and each part stands for a testable claim from team psychology. Because of this structure, for any fitted parameters, a forecast moves away from rest only when task progress or a prompt pushes it, and prompts of bounded size that are spaced in time move it a bounded distance. On four-person teams held out from training, a team that drifts from its usual behavior returns most of the way within half a minute. After 32 s, about 24% of the deviation remains, and ANCHOR predicted 30%. Forecasts are clearly better when the resting point blends its three sources than when it uses one. ANCHOR matches the accuracy of a black-box baseline with about 40,000 parameters. It anticipates conversation collapse with an AUROC of 0.85. In simulation under assumed prompt effects, it removes 2.2 times as much breakdown time per prompt as periodic prompting.

papers.title: Conditional Endorsement: Simulating How Adults with Different Skills Evaluate Canada's National AI Strategy
papers.abstract: Canada's 2026 national AI strategy, AI for All, commits to free AI training for everyone and to expanding business AI adoption, yet it is difficult to anticipate whether these policies will reach adults with uneven skills and circumstances. We ask how adults with diverse skills might rate these policies on support, effectiveness, and personal benefit, how their skills and circumstances shape these evaluations, and what implementation conditions they raise. We built 3,200 generative agents from a weighted sample of the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) Cycle 2 respondents, collected their ratings and explanations for 20 policies, and analyzed dialogues between agents with contrasting ratings. The agents supported nearly every policy but were far less confident that they would improve adult AI literacy or benefit them personally. This gap widened as digital technology use declined: agents modeled on adults who had never used a digital device still endorsed the policies but rarely expected to benefit. Agents traced the gap to participation costs, hard-to-exercise rights, and limited community control, and their dialogues specified these conditions rather than resolving disagreement. We describe this pattern as conditional endorsement and argue that AI literacy policy should be designed and evaluated for adults with the fewest digital skills.

papers.title: Instructor-designed AI improves learning in a randomized trial across 19 universities
papers.abstract: Universities are alarmed by recent evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) can undermine learning, with students prescribed generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools performing worse. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities over three semesters, we tested whether AI designed by frontline instructors can improve learning. We encouraged instructors to design AI solutions they believed would best help their students. Drawing on their unique knowledge of their classes and students, the instructors created a wide array of innovations. We show that these instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning, measured by AI-proof assessments (proctored, in-person examinations). We found no change in student engagement, measured by course activity records, or satisfaction, measured by course evaluations. Our findings demonstrate that AI can improve student learning when its adoption is frontline-driven, with instructors empowered to design and refine AI solutions for their own classrooms.

papers.title: AdaptType: Accessible and Customizable Multimodal Text Entry in Virtual Reality for People with Upper-Body Motor Impairments
papers.abstract: Text entry in virtual reality (VR) is cumbersome, especially for people with upper-body motor impairments. Existing techniques often demand both fine and gross motor control, yet users' motor abilities vary widely. To address this range of needs, we present AdaptType, a multimodal VR text entry system that enables users to configure input techniques that best suit their abilities, and scaffolds customization through ability-based recommendations. Through a study with 10 participants, we found that customized multimodal techniques improved text entry speed compared to gaze- or hand-only techniques, and complemented voice for error correction, decreasing failure rate from 15.1% to 2.0%. We found that AdaptType yielded high text entry speed (36.26 WPM) and accuracy (0.36% error rate), with low task load and high usability ratings. We also found ability-based recommendations effectively scaffolded customization. Our work contributes more accessible and personalized VR text entry solutions for people with upper-body motor impairments.

papers.title: Aspirational Identities: How VTubing Affords New Modes of Digital Embodiment
papers.abstract: VTubing, short for "Virtual YouTubing", is a modality of streaming where a CGI avatar is used in place of the streamer's analog face and body. As VTubing has become increasingly popular, especially for queer and trans streamers of color, it is worth studying as a way for streamers to express identities that they hope to embody, which we call "aspirational identities". In this workshop submission, we draw on preliminary findings from qualitative research to argue that VTubing is a potent object of study for understanding digital embodiment and the performance of identity online, especially for questions of race, gender, sexuality, and disability.

papers.title: B2G-Agent: An LLM-Based Multi-Agent Tool for End-to-End Building-Grid Interactions
papers.abstract: Buildings are major electricity consumers and can interact with distribution network dispatch through flexible power scheduling. These interactions require distribution network operators (DNOs) and building energy managers (BEMs) to reconcile their operational constraints and perform complex cross-field computations. The lack of cross-domain expertise and unified computational workflows could lead to inefficient or physically infeasible interactions. To address this bottleneck, we develop an end-to-end large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent tool, B2G-Agent, that bridges DNOs and BEMs. The tool deploys three collaborative agents: a Translator for bidirectional cross-domain semantic mapping via hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); an Actor for automated configuration and execution of joint simulation and optimization through directed acyclic graphs; and a Reviewer for memory-augmented reflective failure diagnosis. This workflow abstracts away cross-field modeling complexities and enables both sides to focus on high-level operational decisions. Comprehensive evaluations across 200 synthesized tasks show that B2G-Agent improves the interaction quality score from 66.71 to 85.57 and increases the task success rate from 38.0% to 69.0% over the baseline while satisfying operational constraints. The open-source tool and interface are available at https://github.com/hkuedl/B2G-Agent.

papers.title: MemoryLane: Supporting Reminiscence Conversations Between Older Adults with Mild Dementia and Lay Caregivers Using a Simulated AI Agent
papers.abstract: Reminiscence Therapy (RT) is a non-pharmacological intervention that invites patients to discuss and review past life experiences and memories to improve their emotional and mental well-being. In practice, many reminiscence conversations are led by lay caregivers, such as spouses and adult children. While traditional RT often relies on personal photographs, curating them can be tedious and difficult. In addition, caregivers who lack shared life experiences with the patient may struggle to facilitate engaging reminiscence conversations. This paper presents MemoryLane, an AI-integrated tool that helps lay caregivers facilitate reminiscence conversations without curated photographs. MemoryLane supports a triadic conversation among the patient, the caregiver, and a simulated AI agent that acts as the patient's peer. A shared interface shows the agent and AI-generated images of the memories being discussed, while a private smartphone interface lets the caregiver control the behavior of the simulated AI agent and moderate the AI-generated images. A preliminary focus group study with five dementia-care stakeholders suggested the value of MemoryLane's AI agent as a peer companion and of AI-generated images, as well as the feasibility of having caregivers moderate images and control the AI agent.

papers.title: Who Shows Up, Who Benefits, and Who Wins? Expert-Novice Disparities in Team-Seeking Forums and Competition Performance on Kaggle
papers.abstract: Team formation is the first social gate to collaboration in online communities, yet it remains unclear whether public team-formation mechanisms broaden access to collaborators or reproduce existing hierarchies. We examine this question on Kaggle, a data science competition platform whose "Looking for a Team" (L4T) megathreads let participants publicly seek teammates for on-platform competitions. Grounded in Communities of Practice theory, we conduct two complementary studies of 18 competitions held in 2023. Study 1 analyzes the reply network among 671 megathread participants and finds that 89.3% are low-tier users, yet higher-tier users receive significantly more replies (Kruskal-Wallis H=16.46, p=.00246) and achieve higher rates of forum-visible teaming success (52.9% vs. 32.6%; chi-squared=10.53, p=.001), a proxy for eventual team membership. Linking megathread posters to verified team rosters from 16 competitions partially supports this proxy. Twenty-six final teams contained two or more megathread posters, indicating that megathread interaction sometimes, but not always, maps onto realized teaming. Study 2 links participation traces from 219 users to private leaderboard outcomes and finds that productive participation (submission count rho=.435, cross-competition participation rho=.247) is positively associated with performance, whereas megathread-specific discussion is not (rho=-.021). The submission-performance association appears stronger in higher tiers, although the novice subgroup estimate is imprecise. Together, the findings suggest that open access to team-seeking forums does not guarantee equal participation. Visible expertise shapes who attracts attention, and engagement in the community's core practice is more strongly linked to success than discussion alone. We discuss implications for designing more equitable team formation in online collaboration environments.

papers.title: Between Rigor and Reality: How AI Safety Benchmark Developers Understand Benchmark Use and Maintenance
papers.abstract: Safety benchmarks are cited as the primary tool to understand the risks posed by generative AI (GenAI) systems, yet growing evidence suggests they often fail to meet the needs of real-world safety evaluation. We present findings from five interviews with AI safety benchmark developers in academia and industry. We find a disconnect between perceptions of the intended usefulness of safety benchmarks and their practical usefulness in safety evaluations of deployed systems. Our participants offered perspectives on two challenges contributing to this disconnect: (1) the difficulty of achieving inter-rater reliability on safety constructs, and (2) a lack of clarity regarding how to address persistent threats to external validity. Based on our analysis, we argue that safety benchmarks must not only be grounded in deployment contexts, but actively integrated with them. To facilitate this, we outline pathways for more transparent communication between academic and industry AI safety stakeholders.

papers.title: Dependable Voice Command for Multi-UAV Swarms Using Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Supervisory control of multiple autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) imposes high visual and cognitive demands on human operators, particularly when communicating mission objectives and system constraints. Voice command provides a natural interaction modality that can reduce operator workload; however, its reliability is affected by environmental noise, speech variability, and recognition errors. This paper presents a dependable voice command framework for multi-UAV swarm supervision using Small Language Models (SLMs). The proposed architecture integrates an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) module with an SLM-based semantic processing layer to transform spoken operator commands into structured task definitions for downstream multi-UAV planning and execution. To evaluate robustness, an end-to-end assessment pipeline is developed using a Probabilistic Context-Free Grammar (PCFG) to generate synthetic supervisory commands, which are converted into audio samples with varying operator accents and environmental signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). The resulting speech signals are processed by the ASR module, and the SLM performs contextual interpretation and phonetic correction of transcriptions when required. The evaluation isolates the resilience of the voice command pipeline under acoustic degradation and speech variation, demonstrating reliable task generation for multi-UAV supervision in challenging operational conditions.

papers.title: Between Obligations and Evidence: A Participatory Study of Translating the EU AI Act into Technical Requirements
papers.abstract: The EU AI Act imposes technical and organizational requirements for high-risk AI systems, but applying these requirements involves contextual choices about what to measure and what evidence supports a compliance claim. We investigate these challenges through a participatory workshop involving 32 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners from different disciplines, using realistic scenarios in healthcare, recruitment, and public transport to examine how regulatory obligations are interpreted, translated into technical requirements, and evaluated in practice. Through a thematic analysis of workshop data, we identify recurring tensions between how regulatory obligations are translated into measurable system properties, how responsibility and human oversight are exercised in practice, and how the validity of compliance evidence is affected by changing operational conditions and system uses. For example, participants highlighted how fairness metrics could conceal discrimination in recruitment, how time pressure and limited information could undermine human oversight in public transport, and how changes in patient populations could invalidate previously established evidence of system performance. Our findings suggest that technical, organizational, and evidentiary challenges are interdependent, and that establishing and maintaining compliance requires attention not only to technical assessments but also to how AI systems are used, governed, and monitored over time. We discuss implications for supporting context-sensitive and ongoing compliance.

papers.title: Toward On-Device Markerless 6DoF Tracking of a Physical Manipulative on a Mixed-Reality Headset: A Preliminary Study
papers.abstract: AR-Classroom uses physical models and virtual overlays to help learners explore spatial transformations. To align these overlays on a standalone headset, we developed a markerless six-degree-of-freedom(6DoF) tracker for a LEGO airplane on the Meta Quest 3. A compact YOLO model trained on synthetic Unity renders predicts 20 keypoints from dynamic RGB crops resized to 128 by 128 pixels. A perspective-n-point solver estimates the airplane's pose from these predictions and the corresponding 3D landmarks. In a paired evaluation on 1,000 synthetic validation images, cropping guided by ground-truth boxes increased the detection rate on annotated images from 32.5 to 46.2 percent. Mean keypoint F1 increased from 42.9 to 44.6 percent, with lower keypoint precision in the cropped view. In preliminary headset tests, 2 Hz was the highest tested tracking target at which the application maintained approximately 72 frames per second. A headset demonstration illustrates virtual overlay alignment with the physical airplane before and after a manual rotation. Quantitative 6DoF pose accuracy on real headset footage will be measured in future work.

papers.title: Voice-Based Conversational Agents as AI Care Assistants: Evaluating Personalization, Intervention Delivery Fidelity, and Privacy Expectations in Older Adults' Care
papers.abstract: Generative AI enables voice-based conversational agents to play more active roles in older adults' care, including personalizing support and operating alongside clinicians and care partners. This shift creates two challenges: how to personalize support while faithfully delivering evidence-based interventions, and how to manage personal-data use and sharing across AI and care stakeholders. We designed and evaluated ARC, a voice-based conversational agent that operationalizes multidomain lifestyle intervention through sessions with predefined goals, participant context, and evidence-based components. In a 3-day remote study, 80 older adults completed 473 sessions across six session types (9,183 turns; averaging 19.4 turns and 6 minutes per session). Participants reported favorable usability, acceptability, and use intentions. System-level analyses showed strong domain-level but modest participant-specific contextual reuse, no significant personalization-fidelity association, and fidelity limitations centered on incomplete delivery of intervention components rather than off-protocol drift. Within care relationships, expectations for personal-data use and sharing varied by data type and recipient. Our findings support feasibility of conversational delivery of multidomain lifestyle intervention, offer methods and system-design insights for longitudinal evaluation, and motivate an evaluation agenda for generative AI health interventions: user-experience and outcome measures should be complemented by evidence of whether intended intervention processes were delivered as designed.

papers.title: Clean Tickets, Wrong Orders: Catching Silent Errors with a Language Model in Your Browser Tab
papers.abstract: A small language model that turns a typed order into structure can fail in two ways. It can print something broken, which any system rejects. Or it can print a clean, well formed order that nobody placed. Our companion work calls the second kind a silent error, and it is the dangerous one. We present a web demo in which a fine-tuned 0.8B parameter model runs entirely inside the visitor's browser tab, through llama.cpp compiled to WebAssembly. No order text leaves the device. The page parses orders as the visitor types, scores every ticket with the PIZZA benchmark's own matcher ported to TypeScript, refuses anything off the menu with "?" so the model can face the open web, and lets visitors hunt for silent errors or try to cause one. Run in the browser on all 1,357 PIZZA test orders, the deployed model writes the same output as the server evaluation for 99.0% of them and reaches the same exact match (0.882); we also report its latency on 3 consumer laptops. Demo: https://wrong.cuyor.com

papers.title: Personalization of Basic and Moral Values Guiding LLM-Controlled Assistant Robots
papers.abstract: Personal assistant robots powered by large language models (LLMs) are likely to enter everyday life within the next decade, but the values that should guide their behaviour remain largely unspecified. Current alignment practice steers a single model toward an aggregate of human values, ignoring that individual users may prefer a robot whose value profile differs from their own. We administer parallel self- and robot-targeted versions of three established psycho-metric instruments - the simplified Schwartz Values Survey (SVS), the Portrait Values Questionnaire (PVQ-21), and the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ) - to potential future users (N=22), capturing both their personal values and the values they would want an assistant robot to embody. We compare the three instruments as personalization tools using the UEQ-S and benchmark fifteen contemporary LLMs against the resulting profiles. Participants wanted their robot to score markedly lower than themselves on personal-focus values and higher on social-focus values; moral profiles were nearly identical. LLMs prompted to act as robots shifted only weakly toward the desired profile, indicating that default model behaviour and prompt engineering are no substitute for explicit value personalization.

papers.title: What a Memory Preview Cannot Tell You: Ambiguity in AI Memory Permissions
papers.abstract: A memory rule states when an assistant may reuse a remembered event, and an editor can confirm a rule by previewing one use it allows and one it blocks. We ask what such a preview lets a person infer about the rule they saved. For an editor with six or twelve valid rules, we enumerate every rule compatible with a preview. Splitting the rules most evenly does not target the question a user cares about. For an explicit preference, two adaptive tests leave all three recommendation scopes open (for a one-off choice the outcome turns on a tie), while one test of transfer to another task settles the question. Weak previews are also the default. Under the intended rule, 36 of 39 possible allowed/blocked pairs contain a blocked example that no rule allows, and no pair identifies the rule. Three or four tests suffice here; when permissions depend on each other, a fixed checklist grows to six or nine and adaptive questioning needs at most five or seven. These counts use a specified rule vocabulary and fictional events. In a small pilot, 10 of 20 people who saw such a weak preview of a rule they had just chosen mispredicted, or were unsure about, at least one of two uses, and none of those 10 said the outcomes matched what they wanted. Whether better previews help people is untested.

papers.title: DECODE: Diagnosing Interpretability Failures in Automated Interpretation Process
papers.abstract: Tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on LLMs themselves to both generate and evaluate explanations, creating a self-referential automated interpretation process with minimal human oversight. This automation raises significant reliability concerns, which are exacerbated by the absence of ground truth. In practice, it is difficult to validate explanations or to attribute interpretability failures to their source -- whether they originate from the tool's extracted representations or from the LLM used in the process. To address these challenges, we present DECODE, a visual analytics system that reintroduces human oversight into the automated interpretation process. Our approach decomposes the diagnostic workflow into three progressive stages, isolating failure sources ranging from structural defects to explanation-level misalignments. Drawing inspiration from inter-coder consensus in qualitative analysis, we utilize consensus among independently generated explanations and their evaluation metrics as a proxy for reliability. To further scale human inspection, we employ a three-phase active seeding protocol that strategically recommends high-priority instances for manual review. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features, showing that it can efficiently identify and attribute interpretability failures at scale.

papers.title: Alleviating Interview Stress: Effects of Robot Persona and Reactive Backchanneling on High-Pressure Mock Interviews
papers.abstract: High-pressure job interviews induce anxiety and impair performance. Existing mock training suffers from a trade-off among cost, standardization, and physical presence. This study investigated how a robot interviewer's verbal persona (supportive vs. challenging) and nonverbal backchanneling (active vs. negative) affect users' psychological states and facial expressions in a simulated interview. In a 2x2 between-subjects experiment (N=28), participants interacted with a NAO robot. Subjective measures (state anxiety, self-efficacy, social presence) and objective facial emotion recognition were collected. Results showed that a supportive persona reduced task load, increased perceived robot warmth and mind perception, and decreased perceived surveillance and robot discomfort. Active backchanneling increased non-neutral (p = .021) and anxiety-tension facial affect (p = .048). A significant interaction effect between persona and backchanneling was found on social presence (p = .045). The subjective-objective consistency was 67.9%, indicating complementary measurement modalities. The findings provide preliminary support for the social buffering hypothesis in human-robot interaction.

papers.title: Multimodal Person Concept Model for Person Identification under Varying Observation Conditions
papers.abstract: Service robots in domestic and office environments must identify users to provide personalized services based on their preferences and previous interactions. This is challenging because only a few observations may be available for learning, while observation conditions change owing to appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content. To address this challenge, this study proposes a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of observations, without person labels, and enables robust identification under changing conditions. The model employs a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process and integrates visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted using Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP), followed by principal component analysis (PCA). We evaluated six participants under eight conditions in which appearance changes, additive noise, and transcription errors were introduced individually and in combination. Averaged over the eight conditions, the proposed model achieved an identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of person concepts from the observations, which is comparable to k-means clustering that was supplied with the true number of participants (0.88). We also examined PCA dimensionality, modality availability, and variation strength, and demonstrated the model on a Toyota Human Support Robot. These results show that multimodal person concept learning supports robust person identification under changing conditions, and that identification can succeed even when the number of concepts is not correctly recovered. The project page and demonstration video are available at https://okitamisan01.github.io/person_concept/.

papers.title: DesignSpecs: A DESIGN.md Dataset of Visual Design Specifications for AI Agents
papers.abstract: While AI agents increasingly generate and modify user interfaces, they rarely rely on a visual design specification for a certain project. The DESIGN$.$md format, which originated from Google's AI design tool Stitch and which was open-sourced in April 2026, addresses this gap by describing a visual identity through design tokens (such as named colors, text styles) and Markdown prose. To our knowledge, no large-scale research dataset of such design specification files exists. We present DesignSpecs, a dataset of 36,906 DESIGN$.$md files from 15,794 public, non-fork GitHub repositories, representing 17,240 unique file contents. We collected 613,207 files named DESIGN$.$md in October 2026. Because the same file name also denotes architectural plans and other design documents, we filtered those with YAML front matter, a design-system name, at least one recognized design token, and zero errors under the official linter. Our JSON Lines dataset provides file-level and deduplicated views of the original Markdown, links files to repositories, paths, and commits, and is released with related scripts. We outline research opportunities on visual design knowledge and design-aware AI agents. Dataset is available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jl-wei/DesignSpecs

papers.title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
papers.abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

papers.title: Learning Recommendations under Imperfect Human Compliance with Record-Level Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: This paper investigates human-in-the-loop recommendation systems, where effectiveness relies on human compliance and privacy concerns restrict the use of historical response data. The pro posed framework models the implemented action as a random response to the recommendation and formulates the recommendation mechanism as a decision-dependent optimisation problem under an unknown compliance distribution. A batched Gaussian process upper confidence bound algorithm is then adapted to learn from locally perturbed historical actions, providing privacy for individual raw records. The analysis establishes record-level differential privacy and derives high-probability simple regret bounds when the compliance distribution is unknown. These bounds characterise how privacy noise, batch size, and behavioural information affect the guaranteed quality of the learned recommendation. In particular, a known upper bound on the non-compliance rate enables the rec ommendation space to be screened before any private data are queried. Simulations of a fixed-state car-following problem with synthetic historical driver responses demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm and verify the theoretical findings.

papers.title: A Compact xDAWN-Guided Spatio-Temporal Network with Filter-Bank Convolution for P300 Detection
papers.abstract: P300-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable communication by decoding stimulus-evoked EEG responses into character selections without requiring voluntary motor output. Reliable P300 detection remains difficult because of low response amplitude and signal-to-noise ratio, while practical spellers require accurate character selection with few stimulus repetitions and low computational cost. We propose a compact deep learning architecture that combines xDAWN spatial filtering for event-related potential enhancement and dimensionality reduction, a fixed frequency-selective filter bank, and convolutional feature learning for spatio-temporal EEG decoding. Depthwise-separable convolutions and progressive average pooling reduce computational complexity while retaining discriminative temporal information. The resulting target/non-target classifier contains only 5,100 trainable parameters. We evaluated the model on two public benchmarks, BCI Competition II Dataset IIb and BCI Competition III Dataset II, and compared it with established P300 decoding methods across different numbers of stimulus repetitions. The model achieved an information transfer rate of 17.8 bits/min with two repetitions on BCI Competition III and 40.5 bits/min on BCI Competition II, demonstrating a favorable accuracy-speed trade-off. These results suggest that combining domain-informed spatial and spectral priors with compact neural networks can support efficient P300 decoding for EEG-based BCI communication.

papers.title: Neural Representations as New Modes of Interactivity
papers.abstract: Human-AI interaction today runs almost entirely through prompts and outputs, keeping AI systems opaque to general users. We introduce Neural Representation Interaction (NRI), a paradigm that treats the internal representations of neural networks as an interaction material people can inspect, steer, and edit. Situating NRI alongside graphical, tangible, and bio-computer interaction, we argue that the concepts and algorithms models encode internally offer representational affordances for richer human-AI interaction. We synthesize actionable mechanistic interpretability methods and, drawing on General Morphological Analysis, construct a design space spanning Interaction, Target, Referent, and Purpose. Mapping existing interfaces onto this space reveals that most serve expert auditors, while few support lay users. We then present speculative applications in education, personal user modeling, and hiring audits, and discuss design principles, limitations, and sociotechnical risks. NRI offers HCI researchers abstractions for designing interactions that work with AI computation rather than only through its inputs and outputs.

papers.title: Exploring Socially Acceptable 3D Feedback Design for Inclusive Small-Group Conversation
papers.abstract: Prior research has shown that providing feedback on group dynamics can improve the quality of small-group conversations. However, publicly delivered feedback that targets specific individuals may reduce social acceptability due to negative experiences such as social pressure, embarrassment, and resistance. This work investigates how public feedback can be designed to remain socially acceptable while maintaining its effectiveness in XR-based small-group conversations. Informed by social science and HCI literature, we identified three design strategies (incorporate humor, reduce social attention, and use indirectness) and proposed a set of metaphor- and agent-based 3D feedback probes. We then conducted a two-phase study: (1) an online survey with 50 participants to examine how such feedback designs are perceived under public and private delivery, and (2) follow-up interviews with 14 participants who completed the survey to better understand their interpretations and elicit additional insights. Results show that metaphor- and agent-based feedback can reduce social discomfort while maintaining effectiveness. Interview findings further highlighted the role of three strategies in making feedback easier to accept, while requiring careful balance. We also discussed design implications for creating socially acceptable 3D feedback to support inclusive small-group conversations in XR.

papers.title: DiffSSMEye: Conditional High-Frequency Eye Movement Synthesis with Structured State-Space Diffusion
papers.abstract: Synthesizing high-frequency eye movements requires preserving long-range temporal dependencies and subject-specific oculomotor dynamics. However, methods based on generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs) can struggle to preserve these characteristics simultaneously. We introduce DiffSSMEye, a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model with bidirectional Structured State Space Sequence (S4) layers for generating five-second gaze-velocity sequences at 1,000 Hz. Generation is conditioned on a coarse gaze reference, user identity, and task, where identity and task embeddings are incorporated through feature-wise linear modulation. Identity-preservation, multi-resolution spectral, and integrated-drift losses complement noise prediction to constrain biometric consistency, frequency structure, and displacement error. Subject-disjoint evaluation on GazeBase across seven tasks yields mean real--synthetic embedding cosine similarities of 0.91--0.95. DiffSSMEye also achieves the lowest median spatial errors among these baselines for horizontal and random saccade tasks. These results demonstrate improved spatial accuracy and biometric feature consistency for subject-specific gaze synthesis.

papers.title: It Was Better Not to Know: Digital Recognition, Family Authority, and Postpartum Mental Health in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Postpartum mental distress affects roughly one in five mothers in low- and lower-middle-income countries, yet recognition and support remain limited where formal mental-health care is scarce, and family relationships govern health decisions. We report a five-month interview study with 20 mothers in urban, urban slum, and rural Bangladesh who had given birth within the previous two years. Mothers encountered the concept of postpartum depression incidentally, through Facebook and YouTube recommendations rather than deliberate search or clinical guidance, and then used these platforms for private sensemaking without disclosing. Recognition, however, rarely traveled beyond the self: mothers could identify their distress while families dismissed it, leaving them with knowledge but no authority to act. Participants sought validation as a precondition for support and described recovery as relational rather than clinical or digital. We argue that postpartum technologies should engage partners, families, and community health workers rather than placing recognition solely on mothers.

papers.title: Beyond Curiosity: Habit and Organizational Learning Capability as Predictors of Shadow AI
papers.abstract: Generative AI has entered the workplace faster than organizations can govern it. Employees may use AI tools their employer has not sanctioned and conceal that use, but the psychology of this behavior remains poorly understood. We compare an exploratory-disposition account with one centered on reported use and habit. Using survey data from 510 employed adults reporting workplace generative-AI use during the preceding 12 months, we estimated the unique and relative contributions of workplace curiosity, habit, technology-acceptance beliefs, and perceived organizational learning capability through hierarchical regression, bootstrap relative weights, and full-subset dominance analysis. Habit had the largest relative weight, accounting for 28.3% of explained variance, and completely dominated joyous exploration across all 512 possible predictor subsets. Joyous exploration contributed 3.4% and became nonsignificant when use behavior, performance expectancy, and social influence entered the model; habit subsequently explained additional variance. Organizational learning subscales accounted for 24.1% of explained variance; experimentation and knowledge transfer were associated with lower shadow AI, while curiosity-by-learning interactions were nonsignificant. Separate models for unauthorized use and concealment reproduced the habit-dominance pattern. Perceived professional support was associated with lower concealment, although its coefficient did not significantly differ between the two behavioral outcomes. Shadow AI in this sample was more strongly associated with self-reported habit strength and perceived organizational conditions than with exploratory disposition. The cross-sectional design does not establish causal or temporal order.

papers.title: A Connectionless Interaction Model for Network Spatial Proximity Services
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a connectionless interaction model for network spatial proximity services. In the network spatial proximity model, the reception of an identification or discovery frame of a nearby wireless node confirms proximity and delivers content at the same time. Current Bluetooth and Wi-Fi specifications and mobile platforms extend this one-way announcement with responses, addressed messages, scheduled group exchange, and relaying, which still do not require a connection. The proposed model describes such interaction independently of a concrete wireless technology. It is based on the roles of nearby nodes, the proximity message as the unit of interaction, twelve pattern properties, and six interaction patterns: announcement, mutual announcement, query-response, addressed exchange, scheduled group exchange, and relay. An exit rule defines when a service should move to a connection-based channel. We analyze how the patterns can be implemented on Android and iOS smartphones through native mechanisms, substitution, composition, embedded bridges, or a step-up to a connection, and we propose a pattern selection method for developers. The model generalizes the earlier network spatial proximity model and refines the interaction primitives of the proximity core. It is illustrated by existing services and systems and supported by published measurements and first-order estimates.

papers.title: People prefer AI to human advice in multi-turn conversations but neither changes incentivised behaviour
papers.abstract: People increasingly ask AI chatbots for advice, yet large language models (LLMs) are sycophantic, overconfident, and can amplify human cognitive biases. In this article, we investigate how people perceive advice from humans versus LLMs and whether AI advice reshapes incentive-compatible donation decisions. Using Carrier, a new experimental platform, we designed an experiment where participants made a donation decision after discussing it with an AI chatbot advisor, another human, or receiving no advice. Participants judged LLM advisors to be significantly more rational, trustworthy, convincing, and sycophantic than human advisors. Analysis of chatlogs showed that LLMs were more engaged than human advisors: they shared more facts and more often stated their opinion and justified their recommendations. Despite this, donation decisions did not vary across conditions.

papers.title: A Dual-Branch Graph and Convolutional Network for Interpretable Movement EEG Classification
